438a1f84586bebc1: NEW YORK: Heavy rain and strong winds battered the northeastern US on Saturday as an unusually powerful autumn storm intensified, forcing the cancelation of hundreds of flights and leaving tens of thousands of people without power.
New York, Boston and Philadelphia were all in the firing line of the "Nor'easter" - so labelled for its northeasterly winds - as authorities warned of potential major flooding and road closures.
"This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic Coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend," the National Weather Service said in its latest forecast.
"Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses," it said.
More than 75,000 customers in New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Massachusetts were without power as of 10am Saturday, according to the monitoring tool poweroutage.com.
New York state governor Kathy Hochul said the storm was bearing down Saturday on coastal areas of New York City and Long Island.
"The rain is underway... Mark my words. Much more is coming," Hochul said in a press briefing, with up to 15cm of rain expected on Long Island over the next few days.
"We expect waves as tall as 20 feet in some areas," Hochul said.
New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani warned residents of the country's most populated city about strong wind gusts and the possibility of downed power lines, saying "Don't travel if you don't have to".
The storm forced the cancellation of hundreds of flights, including 130 at Boston's Logan airport alone, according to tracker Flight Aware.
Major airlines, including JetBlue, United and American, issued travel alerts allowing passengers to change their flights without incurring fees.
The UN, where world leaders are gathered for the General Assembly, urged media outlets covering the event to clear broadcasting equipment from outside the New York headquarters due to strong winds.
'Safety has to come first'
Major cultural events in the region were also called off, including the Global Citizen and All Things Go festivals in New York, and Oceans Calling in Maryland.

"Safety has to come first. This is the first time in 14 years we've had to cancel," said organisers of the Global Citizen event in Central Park, which was meant to feature Lenny Kravitz, Lauryn Hill, country stars Lainey Wilson and Shaboozey, and Alicia Keys.
About five inches of rain was forecast in areas of Massachusetts, including Boston - the equivalent of more than a month's worth of rainfall.

After much uproar surrounding his tour, British pop singer Ed Sheeran's weekend concerts near Boston were canceled due to the storm, which could whip up wind gusts of 105km per hour along the New England coast.
Some coastal areas of North Carolina, Virginia, Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey have already seen flooding this week.
Nor'easters can occur throughout the year but are more frequent between fall and early spring. They are almost always accompanied by heavy rain or snowfall, as well as strong wind gusts.
Earlier this year, a Nor'easter that pummeled the northeast disrupted hundreds of flights and left thousands of homes and businesses without power.
That storm came weeks after the region recovered from a devastating winter weather system that was linked to more than 100 deaths.
e7953bbe3d90de5f: SHENZHEN: Ukraine's Elina Svitolina and Anhelina Kalinina swept aside twice defending champions Italy in the Billie Jean King Cup semi-finals on Saturday, sending the country to the final for the first time and setting up a showdown with Czech Republic.
World No. 48 Kalinina laid the foundation for victory with a 6-3 6-4 win over 18-year-old Italian Tyra Caterina Grant, ranked 102 places below her.

Australian Open semi-finalist Svitolina then faced former French Open and Wimbledon runner-up Jasmine Paolini, but the 32-year-old needed little time to stamp her authority on the match, cruising to a 6-2 6-2 win to seal an unassailable 2-0 lead.
The world No. 7 broke Paolini three times in the opening set and added two more breaks in the second to complete the win in one hour and three minutes.
The victory also gave Ukraine revenge for last year's 2-1 semi-final defeat by Italy. It was achieved despite the absence of world No. 10 Marta Kostyuk, sidelined by a wrist injury.

Ukraine now face the Czech Republic, who booked their first Billie Jean King Cup final outing since 2018. Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova and Karolina Muchova secured straight-sets wins against Spain, keeping the Czechs on course for a 12th title.

Italy lifted the trophy in each of the last two years, including a 2-0 victory over record 18-times champions the United States in last year's final, to take their tally in the premier women's team competition to six titles.-Reuters

Lewis used a continuous one-shot technique for the chase sequence, while making use of the iPhone 18 Pro's camera features to create focus transitions as the camera moved.
The Proton Iswara was introduced in 1992 as an updated version of the Saga Megavalve and was previously exported to the United Kingdom.
In the UK market, the model was known as the Proton Mpi.

3d51011153332214: BAKU: World champion Lando Norris on Saturday said Alpine's Franco Colapinto should face a race ban for causing the crash that took him out of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
The frustrated 26-year-old McLaren driver, running in the top ten, added that his race was wrecked by "some drivers who shouldn't be in F1."
Colapinto apologised to both Norris and his Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly for his error when he crashed into them on lap 35 after a re-start following a Safety Car intervention.
"It was a big mistake and I am really sorry," the Argentine said. "Very sad and very disappointed."
Norris said: "I think the (ruling body) FIA should be more strict and start handing out bans for this kind of stuff. It's just careless from people.
"It costs a lot of money – all my car parts are in the bin now. People should just be banned because that's not driving that deserves to be in Formula One."
Norris declined to support claims that race leader George Russell of Mercedes had been too slow on the re-start and allowed the field to bunch up too much.
"George can do what he wants," he said. "In Formula One, I think you expect drivers to anticipate things, to know the grip is going to be low and to know the tyre temperatures are low...
"And they weren't even that low! In F1, you want to be against the best drivers in the world and when stuff like this happens, it's because... well, he shouldn't be there."
Colapinto admitted: "I was completely out of control. So, not a lot more to say than sorry to the team, to Pierre and of course to all in the factory. I'm sorry to Lando also..."
Norris added: "It was a tough race. I was slow on the straights and it was an impossible race with the straight-line speeds.
"At the end of the day, I got taken out – just some drivers shouldn't be in F1 to be honest. Maybe Malaysia will be better for us."
Gasly said: "It was one of the best race cars of the season and we had both of us in the points.
"It is not easy (with a team-mate), but it is all about respect and as long as there is respect everything is possible."-AFP
3d534dbba981e738: MANCHESTER: Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said the club remained confident of proving their innocence, a day after media reports that City had been found guilty of 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules in the long-running case.
In an open letter to supporters on Saturday, Al Mubarak said the process was far from over and City's confidence in proving the club's innocence "is just as strong as when this began."
"Following Friday's media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I," Al Mubarak said.
"Here's what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."
City, who have always denied any wrongdoing, are expected to appeal the decision of the independent panel in a case that has hung over English football for years.

A guilty verdict would rank among the most significant rulings in the sport's history, raising far-reaching questions about financial regulation, competitive integrity and the league's ability to enforce its rules against one of its most successful clubs.
Al Mubarak said he was limited in what he can say about the case because of the strict confidentiality of the legal process.
"Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies," he said.

"I ask you to please carefully read the statement ... which we gave on Friday, and the statement we issued in February 2023 ..." which he included in the open letter. "Every word matters and holds true."

The February 2023 statement said the club was surprised by the alleged breaches, "particularly given the extensive engagement and vast amount of detailed materials that the EPL (English Premier League) has been provided with.
"The club welcomes the review of this matter by an independent commission, to impartially consider the comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of its position."
City reiterated that statement on Friday.
The Premier League has declined to comment.
"It's a confidential process, we're not commenting at all," a spokesperson said.
Al Mubarak asked for patience from supporters.
"While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed," he said.
"We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity."-Reuters
85bd5f12499167b7: From Moaz Nair
With over 5.4 million students packed into educational institutions nationwide, our schools are no longer just places of learning - they have become breeding grounds for systemic violence.

In 2024 alone, reported school bullying cases surged to a staggering 5,703. If that number does not shock you, the global reality should: Unicef confirms that at least one in three children aged 13 to 15 worldwide are subjected to the daily torment of bullying.

This crisis has escalated past name-calling and playground shoves into fatal territories. The starkest reminder of our collective failure is the horrific incident in Kuala Pilah, where a 16-year-old boy was detained under a murder investigation following the tragic death of a 14-year-old student at a school hostel - a nightmare stemming directly from suspected bullying.

Yet, we continue to foolishly shift the blame. Expecting teachers, headteachers, or university chancellors to police the psychological flaws of millions of students at every second of the day is a delusional abdication of responsibility. The problem does not originate in the classroom, and it cannot be solved there.
The mental ruin of the victim

Bullying is not a rite of passage; it is psychological warfare. The trauma inflicts deep, permanent scars, brainwashing victims into a misplaced sense of culpability where they blame themselves for the abuse they suffer. Trapped in a vicious cycle with no visible escape, these children face a soul-crushing sense of powerlessness.

This relentless terror triggers severe anxiety, extreme stress, and clinical depression. In the most devastating scenarios, it drives children even to suicide. Overwhelmed by the crushing weight of their tormentors, victims are effectively paralysed, stripped of the ability to stand up for themselves while the system looks on.
The dysfunctional family catalyst

If we want to stop this menace, we must stop ignoring where it starts: the home. Bullying tendencies do not materialise out of thin air; they are forged in broken domestic environments. A dysfunctional family life is a direct catalyst for hostility, impulsivity, and deep-seated anxiety. When a home environment fails to teach internal conflict resolution, it produces aggressive individuals who project their rage onto peers.

Too often, a bully is simply a product of severe parental neglect - a child throwing violent tantrums as a desperate, toxic cry for attention. Whether it stems from broken homes, domestic violence, or substance abuse, the pattern is identical.
The emotional neglect they experience breeds distorted self-esteem and a learned, hostile reflex. They grow up weaponising conflict because aggression is the only language they were taught at home.
The digital frontier: unchecked cyberbullying

The violence has expanded. Aggression has broken past the school gates and followed our children into their bedrooms through digital screens. Data from Ipsos reveals a horrifying reality: 23% of Malaysian parents report that their children have fallen victim to cyberbullying.

This is not harmless internet drama. Cyberbullying is a relentless, 24/7 campaign of terror that uses mobile phones, chat rooms, and social media platforms to systematically destroy a child. From vulgar threats to compromised pictures and cruel public comments, this continuous digital hostility constitutes severe psychological abuse. Like its physical counterpart, it erodes a child’s sanity and acts as a direct fast-track to attempted suicide.
Stop blaming schools, the defence starts at home

The bitter truth is that these deeply rooted behavioural pathologies start long before a student walks through a school gate. The absolute maximum an educational institution can offer is a reactive, band-aid counselling session for a student who is already broken. Schools cannot cure a rot that started in the living room.

If we want to permanently eliminate this epidemic, the family unit must take centre stage. Parents hold the ultimate power and the primary obligation. While they cannot police every peer group, they can no longer remain passive observers of their children's emotional wellbeing.

Parents must actively cultivate emotional resilience and iron-clad boundaries from day one. The only way to stop a bully - or to keep a child from becoming a target - is to build the defence where it matters most: at home.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

4cbbe05a100578a1: WITH Delhi's choking haze hanging overhead, Peepal Baba presses a young tree into the earth, continuing a nearly half-century mission to restore India's vanishing green cover.

"When I was young, I planted saplings like a soldier," said Swami Prem Parivartan, better known as "Peepal Baba", or "tree father", rubbing earth between his fingers and mixing wet mulch around the sapling's base.
It is the latest tree among millions that his teams estimate to have planted.
"What started as a solitary act of planting became contagious," he said.
At 60, he has turned a childhood fascination with trees into one of India's largest grassroots planting movements.
"We did not wait for governments to act," he said. "We gathered friends, volunteers, wanderers, believers."

In Delhi, a sprawling megacity of 30 million people with scorching summers and toxic winter air, his answer to environmental despair is stubbornly simple — plant a tree, keep it alive, then plant another.
"Whatever little we can do for the environment, we have to do," he said, beaming a warm smile.
Exactly how many trees he has planted, and how much land has been restored, are not his focus.
His trust estimates it has restored vegetation across more than 270,000ha, or 2,700 sq km — more than twice the size of Delhi and nearly as large as California's Yosemite National Park.
The organisation says it has planted or preserved 26 million trees.
But he insists numbers and exact areas are not the point.
"I never counted shade in digits," he said. "It is not about planting one tree or two trees or 1,000 trees. It's about how you manage the land on which those plants have been planted."
His fascination with trees was nurtured by his grandmother and a garden he loved tending.
He planted his first trees on his 11th birthday, including a peepal, or Ficus religiosa, a tree with vast spreading roots, sacred to several of India's religions.
Peepal trees have provided shade for village meetings, temples, tea stalls and markets for centuries.
He calls them "cooling towers of human hope" in his 2026 autobiography.
He put aside a career in academia after university.
Instead, he set off across India by scooter to encourage people to grow trees — and his nickname came from a villager he met while planting.
"Peepal Baba", he decided, carried more authority than "environmentalist", which he regarded as a foreign-sounding word at the time.
"My nickname travelled faster than my scooter," he writes.
That scooter carried him across India multiple times.
From his notebooks, he estimates he travelled nearly 540,000km — enough to circle the Earth more than 13 times.
He slept wherever he found shelter —in temples, homes, bus shelters or beneath a peepal tree.
Long sustained by individual and community donations, the trust has in recent years also brought on major corporate donors to expand its work.
With more than 1.6 million Instagram followers, he now also spreads his message through social media and a growing network of volunteers in the field.
His philosophy has expanded from planting trees to restoring the soil that sustains them.
"Every civilisation that respected its soil prospered; everyone that ignored it perished," he said.
"We've built skyscrapers tall enough to touch clouds, but forgotten how to kneel and touch the soil."
For him, the task remains simple: plant a tree, care for it and make sure it survives.
"When people ask, 'How many?', I answer, 'As many as it takes to give the Earth a second chance'."

4d7b4a64960cc14c: JAKARTA: The death toll after a ferry sank in Indonesia's Java Sea almost two weeks ago has jumped to 64, an official said on Saturday, as rescuers extended the search for dozens still missing.

The Virgo Transport 8 was carrying 213 passengers and 30 crew when it lost contact with its shipping company after departing from Indonesia's second largest city Surabaya on Java island, headed for Banjarmasin on Borneo.
"Out of 243 persons onboard, 172 have been evacuated, 108 survived, 64 died, and 71 are still being searched for," National Search and Rescue Agency official Yudhi Bramantyo told a news conference.
Rescuers recovered four bodies from the submerged ship on Saturday, while seven others were found along the shoreline, Yudhi said.
He added that the search operation would be extended a further seven days but will be evaluated every three days.
Search-and-rescue operations typically last for seven days in Indonesia, and authorities can extend them based on factors including an assessment that some of the victims could still be recovered.
Marine accidents regularly occur in Indonesia, a vast Southeast Asian archipelago of more than 17,000 islands that relies heavily on boat connections for daily transport and tourism.
Lax safety standards and unpredictable weather are often the main reasons for disasters.
f9150760ae649aec: FROM his high-profile address at the United Nations General Assembly to his high-stakes White House summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, United States President Donald Trump this week was looking to reassert himself on the world stage.
But Trump's diplomatic flurry has done little to dispel the view among many analysts of a president beset by problems at home and abroad.
Trump has begun facing pushback from world leaders on issues ranging from the crisis in the Middle East to Russia's war in Ukraine, leaving the impression of a foreign policy agenda that has stalled.
This comes as Trump's Republican Party faces midterm elections in November that could further constrain him politically.
Even so, Trump's speech to the UN on Tuesday was a stark reminder of how he has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped to create from the ashes of World War 2.

Standing atop the rostrum of a world body dedicated to peacemaking, he issued a fresh threat to "annihilate" Iran if it did not agree to a deal, defended his coercive approach to Opec member Venezuela and signalled he may not be done deploying the US military to achieve his international aims.
Despite that strident stance, Trump's talks with Xi on Thursday put the US president up against a Chinese counterpart who appeared to be in stronger position.
Xi's state visit was heavy on pomp and ceremony but light on substance, despite a host of thorny issues such as artificial intelligence, trade, Taiwan and Iran.
The most tangible outcome appeared limited to a two-month extension of a trade truce.
"Trump sees himself taking us back to a world where might makes right," said Brett Bruen, who was a foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration.
"It's noteworthy that he goes all wobbly when it comes to Xi Jinping and ascendant Chinese power."
A White House official said Trump's UN remarks "highlighted his various wins in advancing US interests around the world", including preventing Iran from getting a nuclear weapon.
The war with Iran, which Trump started alongside Israel on Feb 28, has dragged on for nearly seven months, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region.
Iran's defiance has become the most intractable foreign policy challenge of Trump's second term.
Trump used his address at the UN to defend his attack on Iran and to declare that "America is back", stronger than ever.

But after a string of early foreign policy achievements, including a Gaza ceasefire and the capture of Venezuela's leader, Trump's record in his second term in office is increasingly defined by stalemates.
World leaders appear to be preparing for a time when the US president's influence could begin to wane following the midterms, and with less than two-and-a-half years left in office.
Most European and Asian allies have already spurned Trump's demands for assistance in an Iran conflict he launched without consulting them.
At this year's UN gathering, some US partners took aim at Trump, mostly without mentioning him by name.
France's President Emmanuel Macron warned against a global "return to the law of the jungle".

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva decried foreign interference in his country's election next month and insisted that "we do not need aircraft carriers patrolling our waters, we need cooperation to stem the flow of weapons and money that fuel crime".
In another sign of diminished clout, Trump's effort to pressure Ukraine and Russia to agree to even a limited energy ceasefire failed to gain much traction.
And while Trump touted a deal with Denmark and Greenland for an expanded US military presence in the vast Arctic island, it fell short of his initial demand to "own" the territory by force.
"A year ago, few countries dared cross Trump," Ian Bremmer, president of the Eurasia Group, wrote on X. "Now Canada, Europe, China, Iran, Russia and others are all more willing to say no."
At one point, Trump himself seemed to wonder how much international sway he actually possessed.
In his speech, he told world leaders he wanted to rebrand AI as "super intelligence".
"Let's see if I have any power," he said. "Maybe I do and maybe I don't. We're going to find out pretty soon."
The writer is from Reuters

b00b1bd3fd6f2f8d: PETALING JAYA: The Form 2 student who died after being allegedly assaulted by a senior is believed to have been “punished” for breaking the school’s rules, police said.

Negeri Sembilan police chief Alzafny Ahmad said a preliminary investigation revealed that the Form 4 student arrested in connection with the case is believed to have reprimanded and “punished” the victim for his “offence”, Astro Awani reported.
“To date, we have only arrested the Form 4 student to facilitate the investigation,” Alzafny was quoted as saying.
Earlier, it was reported that the 16-year-old suspect was remanded for six days until Oct 1.
The victim, Idlan Fareeq Shahril, was found unconscious in the dormitory of a sports school in Kuala Pilah, before being rushed to Tuanku Ampuan Najihah Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Police are investigating the incident for murder.
Idlan’s aunt had earlier alleged that a senior at the school hostel assaulted her nephew.
Education minister Fadhlina Sidek has since ordered an immediate audit of the school’s safety compliance.
69e6c32d6478150a: For decades, the world's conscientious majority, Malaysia included, have condemned and sanctioned Israel's occupation, bombing and genocide of Palestine. Yet, similar persecution is occurring in Malaysia's regional backyard: Myanmar's annihilation and displacement of the Rohingya.
This stateless Muslim minority populate Myanmar's Rakhine state, on the country's northwestern coast bordering Bangladesh.
Rohingya and Palestinians share uncanny patterns of persecution and state-sanctioned aggression, contrasted only by historical and political circumstances.
The two groups face severe, systemic crises of massive displacement, widespread destruction of homes and strict restrictions on movement.
Both are devoid of state sovereignty and citizenship, attracting critical international scrutiny.
The outcome is international legal action on alleged genocide and human rights violations before the International Court of Justice.

Still, there are differences: the persecution of the Rohingya is ethnic and citizenship-based on a minority within Myanmar. The 2017 military campaign leading to mass killings and village destruction forced 700,000 Rohingya to seek refuge in Bangladesh. On the flip side, the Palestinian nakbah is intertwined with national conflict over territory, sovereignty, occupation, security and competing claims to self-determination.
Plus, the Palestinian nakbah has geographical dimensions, encompassing Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Palestinian refugees and Palestinians who are citizens of Israel.
Yet, the outcome is the same: human suffering, violence, and killings stemming from military interventions.
In Rohingya, the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army are responsible while Israeli state and military actions are central to the Palestinian occupation, displacement and genocide.
While Malaysia has assisted Palestinians through foreign aid and international backing, the Rohingya situation squarely hits home.

Now, Malaysia has called for more global backing to support countries hosting Rohingya refugees. Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan, in outlining the call in New York, implored for a sustainable solution, including pressing Myanmar to implement the Asean Five-Point Consensus.

He articulated that international assistance to host countries is pertinent, but a sustainable solution must address the root causes of displacement. This means resolving citizenship purgatory and formalising conditions for refugees to return safely, voluntarily and with dignity to Rakhine.

Yet, the broader question would be: how long can the crisis be defined as a refugee problem when its basic antagonism remains? Malaysia and fellow host nations cannot bear indefinitely the financial, humanitarian and social responsibilities of the Rohingya crisis.
In their immediacy, the Rohingya and Palestinians' crises are two sides of the same coin.
7cb60407dce2e08b: PETALING JAYA: The defence ministry has launched the National Defence Literacy Programme to boost public literacy on Malaysia's security, defence and sovereignty, as well as educate the public on the roles they can play in these areas.

Defence minister Khaled Nordin officiated the programme's launch at the Sabah International Convention Centre today, with the initiative starting off in the Bornean state before being expanded nationwide.
Khaled said building public resilience had become more important as part of bolstering national defence, especially with the nature of threats evolving beyond conventional security challenges.

“There must be strength and resilience among the people. If this is absent and only the armed forces play a role in ensuring security, defence and sovereignty, it will not provide the same level of strength

“That is why we are organising this programme. We want to build resilience among the people, and when people’s resilience is strengthened, it will contribute towards credible defence and deterrence,” he said when launching the programme.
Khaled said safeguarding the nation's sovereignty was no longer solely the responsibility of the armed forces, but the entire Malaysian society.

With threats on sovereignty extending to climate change, disasters, and even cyberattacks, he said, defence literacy encompassed the awareness, knowledge and skills that every citizen should possess, including understanding the rationale behind defence-related policies and decisions.
This was crucial to ensure Malaysians were not easily swayed by propaganda or provocation, especially with the emergence of threats through social media and other digital platforms.

“We want the public to clearly understand that defence issues no longer begin with the presence of an enemy at our borders or in our waters,” he said, adding that digital devices and platforms posed potential risks to the country's sovereignty if not used responsibly.

The National Defence Literacy Programme will start with various community activities at the grassroots level conducted by the Malaysian Institute of Defence and Security, and National Defence University of Malaysia.
44a2cdc40311913f: PARIS: Pope Leo XIV on Saturday celebrated an open-air mass in front of hundreds of thousands of faithful in Paris after riding in the popemobile along the iconic Champs Elysees to the cheers of vast crowds clutching French and Vatican flags.

The leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics is on a four-day trip to France, a secular country with deep Catholic roots, with his trip stirring enthusiasm and spiritual fervour among the faithful.
In the highlight of the visit's second day, the 71-year-old pope led believers in a mass at Place de la Concorde, where a giant white canopy had been erected to serve as a makeshift altar.
Dozens of screens have been installed to allow worshippers to follow the service.
Some 700,000 people were in attendance, the Vatican said. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops.
Parents arrived with pushchairs and children perched on their shoulders as crowds hoped to catch a glimpse of the pontiff on the first official papal visit to France in nearly two decades.
"We're incredibly lucky," Suzanne Grange, 62, said ahead of the mass.
"We were already lucky enough to see Pope John Paul II in Paris back in 1980," her husband Pascal, 65, added.

The first US pontiff was visiting France seven months before voters choose a successor to centrist president Emmanuel Macron, with the anti-immigration far right eyeing its best opportunity yet to capture the presidency.
A number of politicians were present, including far-right leaders Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella and former president Nicolas Sarkozy.
Macron was not expected to attend the mass and was represented by his wife Brigitte.
'Civilisation of love'
Fifteen-year-old Alix said ahead of the service that seeing the pope would be "really something".
"After all, he's God's representative on Earth," said the teenager who wore electric blue mascara and glittery cross-shaped earrings.
Earlier in the day, the pope met migrants as he visited Maison Bakhita, an association supporting refugees.
He said it was "possible to encounter one another and to live together in dignity and peace".
Leo also stressed the "fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love".
The association said the pope's visit sent a "message" ahead of the April-May election.
'Saints of France'
On Friday, an estimated 300,000 people turned out to see the pontiff as he waved from his popemobile on the way to the Notre Dame Cathedral.
"There is a sense of fervour reminiscent of that experienced over 40 years ago with John Paul II," Francois Mabille, director of the Geopolitical Observatory on Religion, told broadcaster RMC.
On Friday, Pope Leo stressed the need for ethics to avoid an AI-driven "paradise of machines" and, as war rages in Ukraine for a fifth year, urged France to remain a "tireless champion of peace".
He also told young adults at a stadium outside the French capital on Friday night that they were the "saints of France".
In a deeply secular country, only around five percent of France's 69 million residents go to Catholic church services regularly, a survey found last year.
However, while infant baptisms have declined in recent years, increasing numbers of teenagers and adults are being baptised.
After the mass in Paris, Pope Leo will head to Lourdes, a town in southwestern France where, according to Catholic tradition, the Virgin Mary appeared in a grotto in 1858 to a peasant girl.
In Lourdes on Sunday, he will speak with seven victims of clerical sex abuse.
A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as minors in France, over seven decades.
In recent years, further accusations have emerged against charity icon Abbe Pierre and workers at a Catholic boarding school near Lourdes.
For the last leg of his trip, in Metz on Monday, Leo is expected to deliver a speech about peace in Europe.
f151af7f12aca0b0: KOTA BARU: Kelantan Bersatu chairman Datuk Kamaruddin Md Nor said he would leave any decision on his position as a state executive councillor to the state government amid a dispute between Bersatu and Perikatan Nasional (PN).
The dispute resulted in the suspension of PN activities effective Wednesday.

Kamaruddin, who is also the state executive councillor for tourism, culture, arts and heritage, said he would continue carrying out his duties as usual unless instructed otherwise by Menteri Besar Datuk Mohd Nassuruddin Daud.
"So far, I have not heard of any changes. The appointment of Exco members is the menteri besar's prerogative and depends on his discretion. What happens next is beyond my authority.
"In Kelantan, I am the only Exco member from Bersatu," said the Ayer Lanas assemblyman.
Earlier, PN secretary-general Datuk Seri Takiyuddin Hassan reminded Bersatu that the party is part of the state administrations in Kelantan, Kedah and Terengganu, all led by Pas.
It was reported that the Registrar of Societies (RoS) issued an order suspending all PN activities after issuing a notice to the coalition seeking an explanation over a complaint lodged by Bersatu.
RoS said the suspension was made under subsection 13(2A) of the Societies Act 1966 (Act 832), following the notice issued to PN on Sept 22.
However, the department stressed that the notice was not a decision to cancel PN's registration, but was issued to give the coalition a reasonable period to respond to the complaint.
2a2cfa088d10a0fa: KUALA LUMPUR: Defending champions Ng Eain Yow and S. Sivasangari moved within one win of retaining their Asian Games titles, while teenager Danish Iftikhar Roslee created athletics history on Day Seven of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.

Eain Yow and Sivasangari both navigated tricky semi-finals at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena to reach the men's and women's finals, putting them on the brink of defending their Hangzhou 2022 gold medals and earning early qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Sivasangari defeated Hong Kong's Chan Sin Yuk 11-6, 11-8, 11-7 in a repeat of the previous Games' final.
After falling behind 5-1 in the second game, the world No. 5 rallied to control the match and set up a gold medal clash against India's Anahat Singh.
Top seed Eain Yow overcame a strong start from Pakistan's Noor Zaman to post an 11-7, 11-2, 11-4 victory and advance to the final.
However, Malaysia's run in the mixed doubles ended after C. Ameeshenraj-Rachel Arnold suffered an 11-10, 11-7 semi-final loss to Hong Kong pair Toby Tse-Lai Cheuk Nam.
In athletics, 19-year-old Danish Iftikhar Roslee reached the men's 200m final, becoming Malaysia's first finalist in the event at the Asian Games in 44 years.

Danish clocked 20.76s to finish fourth in his semi-final, qualifying as one of the two fastest non-automatic qualifiers and replicating the feat last achieved by Rabuan Pit, who won bronze at the 1982 New Delhi edition.

However, Haziq Akhir missed out on the 200m final after finishing eighth in his semi-final in 21.50, while Armin Zahryl Abd Latif was eliminated in the men's 110m hurdles heats after finishing fourth in 13.92.
Jonah Chang finished seventh in the men's shot put final with a throw of 18.89m.
At the Tokyo Aquatics Centre, 20-year-olds Nurqayyum Nazmi Nazim and Yong Rui Jie secured bronze in the men's 3m springboard synchro with a six-dive score of 345.81 points.
Pandelela Rinong-Nur Eilisha Rania Abrar Raj, meanwhile, missed out on a podium finish after ending up fourth in the women's 10m platform synchro final.
In badminton, Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani and Pearly Tan-M. Thinaah reached the quarter-finals at the Ichinomiya City Municipal Gymnasium.
Sze Fei-Izzuddin produced a solid performance to beat Japan's Takuro Hoki-Yugo Kobayashi 21-19, 21-16 and set up a last-eight clash against Liang Wei Keng-Wang Chang of China.
Pearly-Thinaah took 29 minutes to brush aside Thailand's Napapakorn Tungkasatan-Hathaithip Mijad 21-8, 21-12, moving within one match of guaranteeing at least a bronze medal.
They will face India's Treesa Jolly-Gayathri Gopichand next.
However, men's doubles scratch pair Aaron Chia-Tee Kai Wun were eliminated after losing 21-19, 21-16 to South Korea's Kim Won Ho-Seo Seung Jae in the last 16.
Men's singles players Leong Jun Hao and Justin Hoh were also eliminated.
Over at Karogi Athletics Park, the national cricket team qualified for the quarter-finals after topping Group B when their final group tie against Oman was abandoned because of rain.
Malaysia finished with three points following Thursday's eight-wicket victory over Hong Kong and will face Bangladesh on Tuesday.

In shooting, reigning SEA Games champion Gan Chen Jie became the first Malaysian shooter to reach an Asian Games 50m rifle 3 positions final at the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Gallery, before finishing eighth with 299.1 points.

Chen Jie, alongside Alia Husna Budruddin (583) and Nur Suryani Taibi (576), also guided Malaysia to a seventh-place finish in the team event with a combined total of 1,746, emerging as the top Southeast Asian team ahead of Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand.
Meanwhile, China surpassed 100 gold medals to stay ahead in the standings by raking in 107 golds on Saturday.
In men's hockey, the Speedy Tigers stunned Pakistan 5-4 in Gifu to virtually sealed their semi-final spot.
The Asian powerhouse lead the medal race with 107 golds, 41 silvers and 28 bronze medals, while hosts Japan trail behind with 31-49-49 and South Korea retain third place with 16-21-36.
Uzbekistan (8-17-9), Kazakhstan (8-8-19), Thailand (8-7-9), Iran (7-14-7), Bahrain (7-2-2), North Korea (5-5-4) and India (4-12-14) complete the top 10 nations.
Malaysia are in 12th position with four golds, one silver and seven bronze medals after adding two more bronzes on Saturday.

8ce9d1d0d63622a2: BAKU: George Russell resisted a late charge from Max Verstappen to claim his first lights-to-flag victory with a composed drive for Mercedes in Saturday's thrilling Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The 28-year-old Briton came home just 0.196 seconds ahead of the four-time champion, with his Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar third on his return after a broken wrist, in a race punctuated by two safety cars.

It was Russell's first win on the fast, challenging streets of Baku, his first since the Austrian Grand Prix in June, and the eighth of his career. It trimmed teammate Kimi Antonelli's lead in the drivers' championship to 66 points.
Antonelli finished fifth behind Ferrari's Charles Leclerc after slicing through the field from 16th on the grid. Seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton was sixth in the second Ferrari.
"It's amazing to be back on the top step, so I want to say a big thank you to the team for helping me through a tough moment," said Russell.
"The first half of the race felt pretty plain sailing, getting the gap, but after the safety car I saw Max behind me and I knew it wasn't going to be easy.
"When the yellow flag came out, I lifted off the power and when I came back I had no turbo and Max nearly got me on the line."
Verstappen was philosophical.
"We had a good race," he said. "In the final lap, George lost a bit of boost so that's why I caught up quite a bit. It got close, but it wasn't enough," he added.
Hadjar drove in pain.

"It's been a very long six weeks since I injured myself, but it felt like the right moment to come back. I felt strong and this is my first proper podium finish on pure pace so I am delighted," he said.
Racing Bulls' rookie Arvid Lindblad was seventh, Esteban Ocon eighth ahead of his Haas teammate Oliver Bearman and Williams' Carlos Sainz.

Russell made a near-perfect start from his 12th pole position to draw clear while, behind him, Oscar Piastri took advantage of a slow-starting Leclerc to take second. Antonelli dropped from 16th to 17th.
Verstappen also enjoyed the opening lap and passed both Alpines before powering past Hamilton, Norris, Leclerc and finally teammate Hadjar to rise to third.
The Dutchman was grumbling about his tyres, but Russell on the same medium compound was already five seconds ahead of Piastri on softs.
By mid-distance, Russell led by 10 seconds, but grazed the wall at Turn 15.
'Oh my God! Oh my God!'
Teammate Antonelli was up to ninth as the Red Bulls scrapped for third, making life easy for Piastri in second.
The processional action ended on lap 30 when Williams' Alex Albon crashed at Turn Five, triggering a Safety Car deployment during which the leaders all pitted.
After five laps, the race resumed with the Dutchman passing Piastri at Turn One.
Behind him, Franco Colapinto lunged up the inside but ran out of space entering the next corner.
He locked up and went sideways, pushing Alpine teammate Pierre Gasly into Lando Norris in a McLaren. The three went off the track in a synchronised slide.
Both drivers for the struggling French team were in position for top-10 finishes.
"Oh my God! Oh my God! I don't believe it," said Gasly on team radio, adding a swear word. "So many points gone".
A second safety car came out for three laps. After the restart, Piastri locked up, dropping to 14th and gifting Hadjar third.
Antonelli passed Hamilton with 10 laps to go to take fifth.
de1a01b3943a5cd1: PETALING JAYA: Johor was affected by unhealthy air quality tonight, with four locations in the state topping the air pollutant index (API).
Heading the list as of 10pm was Pasir Gudang with an API reading of 154, followed by Kota Tinggi (153), Pengerang (152) and Larkin (129).
Two areas in Sarawak also recorded "unhealthy" API readings -- the district police headquarters at Serian (117) and Sri Aman (109).
Fifty-six areas nationwide recorded "moderate" API readings, and six had "good" air quality.
An API reading of zero to 50 indicates good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy, and above 300 hazardous.
bdd7ca9b6592af6f: PETALING JAYA: Raja Perlis Tuanku Syed Sirajuddin Jamalullail berkenan berangkat menerima menghadap Menteri Komunikasi Fahmi Fadzil di Balai Mengadap Biru, Istana Arau di sini hari ini.
Berangkat sama Raja Muda Perlis Tuanku Syed Faizuddin Putra Jamalullail.
Turut hadir Ketua Setiausaha Kementerian Komunikasi Abdul Halim Hamzah.

Istana Arau dalam kenyataan berkata majlis menghadap itu menjadi ruang untuk bertukar pandangan mengenai perkembangan semasa dalam bidang komunikasi, khususnya berkaitan kepentingan penyampaian maklumat yang tepat, berkesan dan mudah diakses oleh masyarakat.

Menurutnya, dalam konteks Perlis, kemajuan komunikasi dan keterhubungan digital mempunyai peranan penting dalam merapatkan hubungan masyarakat, memperluas akses kepada maklumat serta membuka lebih banyak peluang dalam pendidikan, ekonomi dan pembangunan komuniti.

"Aspek literasi digital turut menjadi semakin penting bagi memastikan masyarakat, khususnya generasi muda dapat memanfaatkan teknologi secara positif, berhemah dan bertanggungjawab seiring dengan perkembangan landskap komunikasi masa kini," katanya.

Istana Arau berkata pertemuan itu turut memberi penekanan kepada kepentingan memperkukuh ekosistem komunikasi di Perlis supaya manfaat kemajuan teknologi dan akses maklumat dapat dinikmati secara lebih menyeluruh oleh masyarakat negeri itu.

"Perlis sesungguhnya memasang impian besar untuk menjayakan Pelan Bandar Pintar Negeri Perlis 2030 dengan harapan untuk mendapat bantuan daripada kerajaan pusat menerusi pihak Suruhanjaya Komunikasi dan Multimedia Malaysia (SKMM)," katanya.
156eb8d80163ffaa: SABAK BERNAM: Two popular food premises in Sungai Besar were ordered closed for 14 days after inspectors found various hygiene offences during Ops Bersih Premis Makanan yesterday.
The operation, held in conjunction with the district-level Hari Cuci Malaysia, also saw nine compounds issued against three premises inspected.
Among the offences found were cockroaches and rat droppings beside a kitchen refrigerator, dirty drains and an unhygienic chicken-cutting area.

519758910f5f394e: LONDON: Liverpool have appointed Julian Ward as the club's new sporting director.

Ward most recently served as technical director of Fenway Sports Group (FSG), the US-based majority owners of the English football giants, and replaces Richard Hughes, who stepped down from the role at the start of this month.

“The knowledge and expertise Julian brings will only enhance our football operations, while also ensuring (head coach) Andoni (Iraola) is provided with the support he requires as he continues to make such a positive impression as head coach," FSG president Mike Gordon told Liverpool's website on Saturday.

Ward, who first joined the Reds in 2012 to support the club's scouting, recruitment and player development strategy, said: "Having been part of Liverpool’s football operation for more than a decade, I have a full appreciation and first-hand knowledge of the challenge that comes with the position, as well as a clear understanding of the demands and ambitions of this great club".
Hughes's exit came just weeks after Michael Edwards quit his role as chief executive of football.

Hughes oversaw the biggest spending spree in Liverpool's history in last year's summer transfer window, bringing in a clutch of stars including Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Hugo Ekitike at a cost of £450 million (US$611 million).
During Hughes's two-year tenure, former manager Arne Slot led Liverpool to a record-equalling 20th English league title, in 2024/2025.
Last month, FSG sold a nearly 40% stake in the Premier League giants to a consortium including Amazon's billionaire founder Jeff Bezos.

a229d58b39e246cf: PETALING JAYA: Tindakan individu tertentu menawarkan untuk membeli kuota diesel BUDI Madani daripada pengguna lain boleh membuka ruang kepada penyalahgunaan dan ketirisan subsidi, kata Gabungan Persatuan-Persatuan Pengguna Malaysia (Fomca).

Ketua Pegawai Eksekutifnya, Saravanan Thambirajah, berkata subsidi diesel diberikan kepada individu yang layak bagi tujuan ditetapkan, bukannya untuk dijual atau diniagakan kepada pihak lain demi mendapatkan keuntungan.
Beliau berkata jika amalan membeli dan menjual diesel bersubsidi itu dibiarkan, ia boleh mewujudkan pasaran tidak rasmi atau pasaran gelap.
“Lebih membimbangkan jika ada pihak mengambil kesempatan dengan mengumpul diesel bersubsidi dalam jumlah besar untuk dijual semula pada harga lebih tinggi,” katanya kepada FMT.

Terdahulu, kerajaan mengumumkan pemilik berdaftar kenderaan diesel persendirian yang layak di bawah BUDI Diesel kini boleh memindahkan kelayakan berkenaan kepada individu yang benar-benar menggunakan kenderaan tersebut.

Penambahbaikan pemindahan kelayakan itu berkuat kuasa mulai 16 September lalu, membolehkan pemilik berdaftar memindahkan kelayakan kepada ahli keluarga, rakan atau individu lain yang merupakan pengguna sebenar kenderaan.
Bagaimanapun tular di media sosial baru-baru ini apabila terdapat pengguna mencari individu yang ingin menjual lebihan kuota diesel mereka pada harga RM3.20 seliter.
Ketika ini kerajaan menetapkan harga subsidi diesel bagi kenderaan persendirian iaitu RM2.10 seliter bagi semenanjung, Sabah, Sarawak, dan Labuan.
Mengulas lanjut, Saravanan berkata kerajaan sememangnya menyediakan mekanisme rasmi bagi pemindahan kelayakan BUDI Diesel kepada pengguna sebenar kenderaan dalam keadaan tertentu.
“Ia perlu dibuat melalui sistem BUDI Madani dan tertakluk kepada syarat serta kelulusan. Ini tidak bermaksud penerima bebas menjual lebihan diesel atau kelayakan subsidi kepada orang lain,” katanya.
Beliau berkata Kementerian Perdagangan Dalam Negeri dan Kos Sara Hidup (KPDN) perlu memantau perkara itu dan menjalankan siasatan sekiranya terdapat unsur penyelewengan.
Katanya, penyelewengan diesel sebagai barang kawalan boleh disiasat mengikut Akta Kawalan Bekalan 1961 (Akta 122).
“Nasihat Fomca kepada pengguna adalah mudah, jangan melihat subsidi sebagai satu peluang untuk membuat keuntungan.
"Jangan jual atau beli diesel bersubsidi melalui saluran tidak rasmi. Jika terdapat keperluan untuk memindahkan kelayakan kepada pengguna sebenar kenderaan, gunakan saluran rasmi BUDI Madani.
“Subsidi adalah wang rakyat. Setiap ketirisan akhirnya menjadi kerugian kepada negara dan rakyat sendiri,” tegasnya.
FMT telah menghubungi Timbalan Menteri KPDN Fuziah Salleh untuk mendapatkan komen.

7c2c4d9670af53c0: Today, I’m talking with Matthew Prince, who is CEO of Cloudflare. This episode is part of a two-part series on the future of business.

Matthew last joined us on the show about two and a half years ago, at what we thought then was a wild pivot point for the internet — and now it turns out things are even wilder because of AI, and Matthew and Cloudflare are right at the center of it.

Cloudflare found in June that bots made up more than half of internet traffic. That number just keeps going up as more and more AI companies scrape more and more of the web, and now as more and more AI agents try and do things for people on the web. Cloudflare sits between websites and all those agents, and allows website owners some level of control: Owners can block all those AI tools, allow them, or, as you’ll hear, only allow those that might pay money for access.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

So Matthew and I talked about how to control all these bots, what kind of mess they’re making of the web, and what kinds of information might be valuable in the future as some of the payment schemes come into focus. You’ll hear me ask pretty directly if some of the outcomes he’s describing are actually good — Matthew is a thoughtful guy, and his answer is something I’m still thinking about well after we had this conversation.

AI is also upending everything inside of Cloudflare. Earlier this year, the company laid off more than a thousand people — 20 percent of the company — and then Matthew wrote an op-ed about that decision that ran in the Wall Street Journal under the headline, “How I choose which Cloudflare employees to replace with AI.” That’s pure Decoder bait in every single dimension: AI, big controversial decisions, and org charts, all in one.
And one last thing, before we get going: You can subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Matthew Prince, CEO of Cloudflare. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Matthew Prince, you’re the cofounder and CEO of Cloudflare. Welcome back to Decoder.
Thanks for having me.

I’m really excited to talk to you again. It’s been about two years since you were on the show. I was just looking back over that episode and I said something to you like, “it’s a momentous time for the internet.” And I was not even close. It’s now an even more momentous time for the internet.

You are at the forefront of rebooting how companies work with AI. That is the most Decoder bait of all time. I want to talk about bots and the internet and publishers and Google and all the things that you are in the middle of. But let’s start at the very beginning.

Cloudflare is a complicated, important company. The last time you were on the show, you said, “Cloudflare is a service that makes the internet faster and protects it from bad guys.” Is that still how you would describe what Cloudflare does?

That’s usually what I say when I’m trying to answer a question at a cocktail party and I don’t want to talk to the person any more. What I say if I’m interested in talking to the person more is that Cloudflare is trying to rebuild the internet the way it should have been built from the beginning if we knew how important it was going to be.

We run a giant network. We’re in over 350 cities worldwide, literally thousands of data centers. We have equipment running in all those places, and then we do a handful of things. If you’re trying to put an application or content online, we make sure that it’s safe. If you’re a person or an employee online, we make sure that wherever you go online is safe. We help give people the ability to write applications that can scale to an entire internet audience and run on the infrastructure that we have. That’s the fastest-growing part of our business.

We’ve recently started to think about how the business model of the internet is changing dramatically and we’re trying to help shape what that future business model of the internet looks like and make it as healthy as possible.
Can I connect the dots between the business model of the internet, how the internet should have worked, and Cloudflare trying to build the internet as it should have been?

That is different than, “Cloudflare protects from bad guys.” I will note that’s what you said to me last time, which now makes me feel like you don’t want to talk to me at the cocktail party, but that’s fine. That’s a shift. It’s just a notable shift.

The business model of the internet has dramatically changed because of AI, because of bot traffic, because of AI scrapers, the whole thing. Describe what you think the business model of the internet is right now and what it should be.

For at least the last at least 30 years, the business model of the internet has been advertising. It’s not the entire business model of the internet, but it’s really driven all of the growth of the web and built what we all enjoy today, which really is a miracle.

The company that is responsible for that more than any other is Google, which for the last 28 years has really defined that. We all think about it for search, but they really built out all of the ecosystem around advertising online. They bought DoubleClick, they built things like Google Analytics that let you actually see who was coming to your property. It really is the hero of what I call the first generation of the internet and the first generation of the web.

What’s changing though, very quickly, is who is actually using the web, or what is using the web. Last November I was at Web Summit, the big European tech event, and I was asked, “When do you think that non-human traffic — agents and all of those things — are going to pass human traffic online?” We have a lot of data because we see a huge percentage of the internet, so we pulled all of that data and looked at it and said that in the second half of 2027, automated traffic would become larger than human traffic. It felt like a big deal that we could see that for the first time in the internet’s history.

I was asked again at South by Southwest in March of this year, 2026, and we pulled the data again and it had moved up, where it was going to then be the first half of 2027. We’re like, “Wow, this is growing. This AI thing is a big deal and people are using it like crazy and it’s driving a huge amount of traffic.”

I was stunned when just a few months later in May, the team came to me and said, “You won’t believe it, but automated traffic has now passed human traffic online.” And that’s just expanding like crazy. If you extrapolate that out, with the giant caveat that I’ve gone wrong so far in every prediction that I’ve made on this, five years from now, we think that automated traffic will be 1,000 times human traffic online. Not because human traffic is going to decline, we think it’ll stay around the same, but because we’re just seeing such an explosion in all of the rest of the traffic.

The challenge of that is, if you have 1,000 times more traffic, someone’s got to pay for the infrastructure to power that. That’s going to require bandwidth, that’s going to require servers, that’s going to require a lot of things in order to make that happen.

And, the traditional model of how to pay for that, which was advertising, doesn’t work for bots. Bots don’t click on ads. They don’t respond to pretty swirls of paint and what we traditionally think of as a brand. We’ve got to come up with something else that’s going to power that incredible insatiable demand that’s going to be put on the internet going forward. I’m spending a lot of my time trying to think about what that’s going to look like.
When you describe that as a business model, that implies that there’s going to be customers and revenue and profits. And I don’t know if any of that’s true.
There’s certainly a lot of revenue.
Well, maybe for the CloudFlares and the Googles of the world, but for the —

Or for the Anthropics of the world! Anthropic added $10 billion of revenue in a single month. There is enormous demand for these AI services. And if you’re an AI company, what you really need are three things.

You need great talent and researchers. And right now, that’s scarce. Right now we have a scarcity of people who really understand how to build these systems, but that’s going to change. Every single university in the world is standing back up their AI department. We’re training people like crazy. Labor markets are pretty efficient. We’re going to have more and more people coming into the space.

The second thing that you need is chips. You need the silicon to run these things. Today, Nvidia is the best in the world at that, but you’ve got a whole bunch of others, whether that’s AMD or Qualcomm or all the hyperscalers, that are building their own chips in order to power these things. While we have a massive shortage in the availability of silicon and the ability to actually power it up and turn it on, that’s going to change as well.

The third thing that you’ve always needed is the data to feed into all of these different models. And that’s been the one thing that I think is going to go the other direction. Historically we’ve just made the internet completely open and given bots access to all of the stuff that’s being created.

I think that’s starting to change. We’re seeing a shift where more and more of the people who are creating content, really creating information, are saying, “Maybe we’ll give that away for free to humans, but if a bot is coming for it, then bots have to pay for it because they don’t have that traditional give-to-get. We can’t put an ad in front of them and have that be something that allows me to help pay for the content creation that’s there.”

What we’re seeing actually goes back to some of the original protocols of the internet. The 403 protocol, which was written in the very first version of Netscape, was actually payment required, and you actually have to pay for the content that you’re receiving. Oh, excuse me, I said 403, it’s actually 402.

We are working with other leading companies like Coinbase and Stripe in order to say, “How do we make sure that we can allow people who are creating content, people who are doing things online, anyone who’s putting a website up, to say that in exchange for that thousands and thousands and thousands of times more traffic that’s going to come to you, you’re not going to maybe get the advertising revenue that comes from it, but maybe you can get a fraction of a penny every time somebody actually accesses that information.”

Where does that fraction of a penny come from? It comes from the fee that people are going to be paying for their AI agents and other systems that are out there, similar to how a Spotify or an Apple Music works today.
I like that we’re less than 10 minutes in and we’re already at the 1996 dream of micropayments on the web. We’re going to stick with that for one more turn here.

When I said business model, what I was really pushing at was the idea of incentives. So maybe there is some business model for information. You’re going to publish some new information and bots will come and find it and yep, the 402 protocol will come back to life and we’re going to do, I don’t know, crypto micropayments using Stripe powered by Cloudflare. That’s a version of the future that many people have talked about for a long time.

The incentives to stand all that up on the web is the thing that I’m worried about, when I say there’s a business model and customers and revenue. If I stand up a website, and I think most of my customers are going to be bots and not people, I might not do that. I might just start a TikTok channel instead, and then monetize my TikTok audience in whatever way I might want to monetize a TikTok audience. That seems like a really big inflection point right now at this second.

You mentioned Google, and I’ve asked you about this many times. The incentives to put new information on the web just seem to be in permanent decline. It just doesn’t seem like a good idea any more. On the flip side, the web as an application program, it’s like the absolute apex. Every new app that comes out is a web app, or if it’s a desktop app, it’s just Electron. There’s something happening with the web as an application platform that is incredible, and something happening to the web as an information platform that is devastating. And you’re trying to connect those dots, right? You’re trying to say we can change the incentives over here.
What’s a version of the future — maybe it’s microtransactions, maybe it’s not — where the incentives to make the web an information platform are as good as YouTube?

You’ve illustrated a tough to reconcile dichotomy that’s happening right now. If you look at things like the publicly accessible data on Wikipedia contributions, it’s down significantly, because people are like, “What’s the incentive to put information on Wikipedia?” Something that, again, people are doing for a lot of different reasons.

Back in the day, if you were contributing things to Wikipedia, you knew people were at least reading Wikipedia. Now, the interface through which people consume that information isn’t Wikipedia itself. It’s just reading the answer through whatever answer engine you’re using, whether that’s OpenAI, ChatGPT, or Anthropic Claude, or Grok on X or whatever it is. And that means that the people who are the editors of Wikipedia are saying, “Maybe it doesn’t make as much sense for me to do that.”

The flip side of that is, the web as a whole actually had been declining since about 2012. The web grew like crazy in the late ’90s and through the 2000s. Starting around 2012, you really saw it plateauing and actually decreasing, up until about 2025, where something flipped. Starting in about October of 2025, the various vibe-coding platforms made it easy for anyone to create a website, and so more and more people were creating those applications. And as you said, even your desktop application, your mobile application, increasingly is just a wrapper around what is fundamentally a web application.

The growth of the web itself — with really high-quality stuff and a lot more people contributing to it — is faster today than it has been at any time since the early 2000s. That’s the tension between those various things.

What’s unique about Cloudflare is that because we sit in front of more than 20 percent of the web, we have the ability to overcome some of the incentives problems. We can very quickly turn something on and say, “Okay, you have to pay a fraction of a penny in order to get access to this information.” And that can kickstart the beginning of what we need.

If you don’t have something like that, we face a massive tragedy of the commons problem. Let’s say today I ask my favorite AI agent where I should go to lunch.If I were doing research, I might go look at a couple of different menus as an individual. My AI agent today goes and scans every single menu in the local area in order to figure out what’s going on. Only one of those places is going to actually get my lunch dollars. If that just expands infinitely, if there’s no cost to doing that, at some point my agent’s just going to look at literally every resource that’s available everywhere on the internet, and then come back and say, “You know, you should go to Wendy’s.”

That’s an enormous waste. We’ve got to have something saying that there’s a cost every time you load a webpage. There’s bandwidth, there are servers, there are things that are behind that, and someone has to pay for that. If it’s not going to be advertising and it’s not going to be direct commerce, then there has to be something that actually puts some constraints there. We are in a good place to say, yeah, it can be a tiny amount of money, a thousandth of a penny or something like that. But that’s enough that we can actually start to say, okay, that will help pay for the infrastructure.

If you have incredibly valuable content, if you’re a news publisher or you’re an academic, then maybe there’s a premium on top of that that you charge and say, “Hey, I’m not going to give you this content unless you pay even more for it, but I believe that it’s valuable and we can create a market for it.”

In order for that to happen, you’ve got to have a player like us that’s in the market that can kickstart that. But once you kickstart it, we’ve seen from the side of the buyers, the big AI companies, that they’re all willing to do this. We’ve seen from the side of the sellers, the big content creators, that they’re all really excited about this. What’s really been lacking is the technology that links those things together, and that’s what we’re spending a lot of time building.

It feels like the theoretical underpinning of this conversation is the very notion of scarcity itself. I’m an old copyright lawyer, and copyright law for years and years and years had a built-in mechanism to be important, which was that one copy of a CD was one copy of a CD. And if you wanted another one, it was pretty hard to make another copy of a CD. Even when it got easy, you still needed another physical CD-R, and that imposed some cost on how many copies you could make, and then it was hard to distribute them.

All of that went away with the internet. We moved everything to digital files and the burden of making another copy fell to zero. And I think a bunch of consumers expected everything would be free. There’s that famous quote, “Information wants to be free.” There’s a second half of that quote everyone forgets, which is, “Information also wants to be expensive because it’s hard to generate.” And the internet just turned that upside down.

The gating mechanism of physical media, which provided some scarcity, and thus some economic value that you could measure, went away and we decided information should be zero and maybe supported by advertising. There was actually a tension that became valuable, because that was scarce in its way. You’re talking about imposing scarcity with your technology.

We always talk about markets needing supply and demand. That’s not exactly right. You need demand for sure, and you want infinite demand ideally, or as much demand as you can get. Infinite would probably be bad, because then it would be hard to discover price, but you want demand.

And then, you actually want constrained supply. There’s no market for air where either of us are sitting right now, because there’s plenty of air. But if we go scuba diving, then all of a sudden there’s a market for air, because air is constrained underwater, and so you have to buy it in order to be able to do it.

Music is the example that I look to when I think about what this could look like in the future. I flew up to Stockholm to meet with Daniel Ek, who started Spotify, and it was just a fascinating conversation. If you think about the history of music, once upon a time, the majority of music sales were from CDs or albums or whatever it was. And then, along came the internet and along with it, Napster and Grokster and Kazaa, and all of the things that essentially commodified music and made it available for free for everyone. Even if you’re an incredibly law-abiding human, the majority of people were just downloading music because they wanted access to music.

If you go back 23 years, the music industry in total was valued at about $8 billion, which is a lot of money, but it’s not a lot of money for the entire music industry. That’s The Beatles and The Rolling Stones and everything else. But people were like, “We can’t make any money off of this.”
And then, Steve Jobs steps on stage, and announces iTunes and that it’s going to be 99 cents a song, but they include cover art and they’re going to make sure it’s high-quality and all these things.

Friday's blast destroyed the building in Plaka, near some of Athens' most visited sites including the Acropolis and the Temple of Zeus, damaging nearby houses, shops and cars and sending rubble and broken glass as far as three blocks away.
The building was reduced to twisted metal, shattered tiles and concrete, strewn with household items and clothing. — REUTERS
b1aaea6903feded1: KUALA LUMPUR: The revocation of the appointments of 10 Negri Sembilan State Executive Council (Exco) members is valid under the state Constitution, said Attorney-General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar.

Dusuki, when contacted by Buletin Utama, said the state gazette revoking their appointments, made with the consent of Yang di-Pertuan Besar Negri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, took effect on Sept 20.

The revocation came a week after the 10 issued a statement affirming a proclamation to remove Tuanku Muhriz.
However, the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang maintained that the proclamation was invalid under the state Constitution, law and customs.

13572e43ab5b0826: KUALA LUMPUR: Defence literacy must become a core civic responsibility for Malaysians as threats to national sovereignty evolve beyond conventional warfare, said Defence Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin.
He said everyone needed to understand how defence affected their daily lives and how their actions could contribute to or undermine national security.
"It is not merely a secondary or voluntary expression of patriotism, but a shared value that must be understood and mastered.
"Defence and national sovereignty have become, and must be, a moral responsibility that must be shouldered by everyone," he said.

Khaled today launched the Defence Literacy Programme in Sabah, an initiative led by the Malaysian Institute of Defence and Security in collaboration with Universiti Pertahanan Nasional Malaysia (UPNM) to strengthen public understanding of shared responsibility for national security and sovereignty through a Whole-of-Government and Whole-of-Society approach.
He said the programme represented a shift in mindset to reinforce the understanding that national defence was not the exclusive domain of those in uniform.
Khaled said defence literacy was particularly important as threats could now emerge far beyond the country's borders, territorial waters and airspace.
"Threats to sovereignty can be found everywhere; in laptops, mobile phones, digital platforms and social media.
"All these spaces can pose a threat to sovereignty if we are not mature and careful in using them," he said.
He said defence had three key functions in a modern nation — as a fence or shield, an umbrella, and an anchor or foundation.
The first involved safeguarding national borders, while the second protected the country from external elements and poor decisions that could draw it into conflict.
The third function, he said, was where society played a direct role in strengthening the country's foundations through patriotism, tolerance, mutual respect and good values.
Khaled said Malaysians did not need to become soldiers or take up arms to contribute to national defence.
"Instead, they could strengthen the country's resilience by understanding defence policies, remaining informed about security issues and resisting propaganda, provocation and extremist ideologies.

"The National Service Training Programme (NS 3.0), Malaysia's deployment of peacekeepers under the United Nations and major investments in defence assets and technology are examples of areas the public should understand.
"Society must understand the rationale behind all these decisions and support the country collectively," he said.
Khaled also warned against the creation and spread of falsehoods or content capable of causing public panic and fear, saying such behaviour could threaten social harmony and political stability.

He said stronger defence literacy was particularly important in Sabah, given its diverse population, proximity to two neighbouring countries and exposure to security challenges in the South China Sea and Sulu Sea.
Khaled said the ministry and the armed forces would intensify public engagement through briefings, awareness programmes and other initiatives to improve understanding of defence issues.
"We want society to clearly understand that defence issues no longer begin with the presence of an enemy at the border or in the country's waters," he said.

1c67cdbc8f7e4165: KOTA KINABALU: Satu jawatankuasa khas di bawah Jawatankuasa Teknikal Majlis Tindakan Pelaksanaan (MTP) Perjanjian Malaysia 1963 (MA63) perlu diwujudkan bagi mengkaji cadangan penambahan bilangan Ahli Dewan Rakyat dari Sabah dan Sarawak.
Menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri (Sabah dan Sarawak), Mustapha Sakmud, berkata kajian turut meliputi penetapan garis masa untuk ia dilaksanakan.

Beliau berkata jawatankuasa khas berkenaan juga perlu dianggotai wakil Suruhanjaya Pilihan Raya (SPR), Bahagian Hal Ehwal Undang-Undang, Bahagian Hal Ehwal Sabah dan Sarawak (BHESS) serta wakil kerajaan negeri.

“Jadi, kami harap dengan pendekatan ini, kami akan dapat memperincikan garis masa berkaitan dengan penambahan kerusi Parlimen di Sabah dan Sarawak,” katanya ketika ditemui selepas melancarkan buku The Transformative Integrated Living Lab (TILL): From Philosophy to Practice di Pusat Konvensyen Antarabangsa Sabah di sini hari ini.

Pada Selasa lepas, BHESS dan Jabatan Perdana Menteri telah memulakan libat urus dengan SPR bagi membincangkan hala tuju serta mekanisme pelaksanaan cadangan penambahan bilangan Ahli Dewan Rakyat dari Sabah dan Sarawak.

Mustapha berkata perbincangan dengan SPR masih di peringkat awal bagi mendapatkan gambaran mengenai kaedah dan kajian yang diperlukan bagi meningkatkan jumlah kerusi Parlimen di kedua-dua negeri berkenaan.

“Hasil pertemuan itu, SPR memaklumkan bahawa pihaknya mempunyai kaedah tertentu, namun kajian terperinci diperlukan kerana penambahan kerusi Parlimen di Borneo perlu mengambil kira nisbah penambahan kerusi Parlimen di Semenanjung,” katanya.
